title: Sh-B-T
hook: Shabbat, from a root meaning to stop, to cease

segments.voice: Yesterday, Z-K-R: zachor and zikaron. Your line was memory is doing. Whose name did you say aloud? A new week starts today, with three letters that stop. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-six.

One morning in the book of Joshua, the people walk out of their tents and there's nothing on the ground. Through the wilderness journey, bread had come down from the sky and lay on the ground in the mornings. Now they've crossed into the land and eaten its grain, and the text says it plainly: "And the manna ceased on the morrow." No miracle announced. No speech. It just stopped. The verb for ceased there is built from the same three letters as a word you may already know, a word for a whole day of the week. Today we open it.
screen: `NO MANNA ON THE GROUND.` → `THE MANNA CEASED.` → `THE SAME THREE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Sh-B-T. Shin, bet, tav. Shabbat. Turn it four ways. First, creation. Genesis says God finished the work, "and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made." Rested, in the English. In Hebrew, the verb is from this root: stopped, ceased. The text doesn't say God was tired. It says the making stopped. Second, the opposite promise. After the flood, God tells Noah that "day and night shall not cease." Shall not cease: the same root again. So the world's rhythms never stop, and inside them, once a week, people do. Third, who stops. The commandment in Exodus doesn't stop at the person keeping it. It lists the son and the daughter, the servants, the animals, and "thy stranger that is within thy gates." Shabbat isn't a rest for those who can afford it. Everyone in the household stops together. Fourth, stopping is a skill. The rabbis of the Mishnah gave whole chapters to defining what counts as work on Shabbat, so that stopping could be clear and shared, not a vague good intention. Notice the name. The day isn't called after what people do on it, the meals, the prayers, the songs. It's called after what they stop. Ceasing comes first, and the rest grows in the space it leaves.
screen: `THE MAKING STOPPED.` · `DAY AND NIGHT SHALL NOT CEASE.` · `EVERYONE IN THE HOUSE STOPS.` · `STOPPING IS A SKILL.` · then, large: `TO STOP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop for a minute, and then a little more. Put down whatever is in your hands. If a screen is open behind this one, leave it alone. Sit back. Notice the urge to do the next thing, and don't do it. Let your hands rest, empty. Each time your mind starts making a list, let the list stop, the way the manna stopped: no speech, no fuss. Just ceasing. If you pray, you can hold the word Shabbat on the breath, in and out. The bell holds the time.
Sh-B-T. Shin, bet, tav: to stop, to cease. The root of Shabbat, and of the manna that ceased. Today's word.
Your line: to stop. Today, pick one moment, and stop completely for one minute: no phone, no task, no plan. Let the world's rhythms carry on without you. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Jews who keep Shabbat stop work from Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall, and the rabbis' detailed categories of work, set out in the Mishnah and Talmud, guide what is set down for the day; practice varies across communities.

original.note: Hebrew: the Sabbath; from the root shin, bet, tav, to stop or cease.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shabbat means a day of rest.
what it means: the root means to stop, to cease: the day is named for what stops.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 2:2's 'rested' is vayishbot, he ceased; the same root says the manna ceased in Joshua 5:12.
